summary: Registers the ENUM service type pstn, with subtypes tel and sip, to help route telephone calls in countries where telephone numbers may be moved between carriers. Registration follows the process defined in RFC 3761.

plainLanguage.summary: When phone numbers can move between companies, you need to look up who holds one now. This note registers a lookup label in the ENUM system that points to the information needed to route the call.

questions: enum service for number portability routing
what does npdi mean in a tel uri
how does enum help number portability
subtitle: ENUM labels that point to phone-network routing data, including where ported numbers now live.

tldr.problem: When subscribers keep their phone numbers after changing provider, the dialed number alone no longer says how to route the call on the PSTN, and routing data is spread across many sources.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the Enumservice type "pstn" with subtypes "tel" and "sip", so a NAPTR record can return a URI carrying PSTN routing data such as a routing number and a number portability dip indicator.
tldr.outcome: Providers could answer routing questions with a single ENUM lookup that gives either an on-net (IP) or off-net (PSTN) result. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 4769 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6118. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a PSTN Enumservice
sections.content:
Number portability lets subscribers keep their numbers when they change provider, move, or change services. In countries such as the United States and Canada, naming and addressing on the PSTN have been separated. A ported number is not directly routable and must be translated into a routing number. Other numbers are assigned to carriers in large blocks or pools and can be routed directly. Portability and numbering data are distributed in many formats around the world.

The Enumservices here could let providers place ported numbers, pooled numbers and number blocks, with their PSTN contact information, in ENUM databases that are externally available or heavily cached locally. A provider could then fold all of its number lookups into one ENUM lookup that yields an on-net (IP-based) or off-net (PSTN-based) response.

The type pstn indicates PSTN routing data. This covers number portability data, non-ported numbers (single or in blocks) and other PSTN-oriented data tied to E.164 numbers. It is for numbers that do not designate an endpoint on the public Internet or a private IP network, so they are routable only through the traditional PSTN, even when the call starts on an IP network.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your friend moves house but keeps the same phone number. A caller needs a way to find the new place. This label points to that lookup.

sections.title: Types, Subtypes and Data Distribution
sections.content:
By convention in this family of specifications, the type is the generic part that defines the service, and the subtype names the URI scheme. When a service has just one URI scheme, another may be added later, so the subtype is needed to identify the exact Enumservice.

The URIs returned may use the TEL URI parameters from RFC 4694, and implementations must be prepared to accept them.

Number portability data is often tightly restricted by contract or by a National Regulatory Authority, so these NAPTR records may or may not sit in the e164.arpa tree. The authors think private distribution is more likely. Options are private distribution inside a provider or between parties with access controls, open availability, or distribution by a number portability or industry organization, possibly nationally under regulatory policy. A national authority might even bar the data from crossing the country's borders.
sections.plainLanguage: The big label says phone network. The small label says how to write the address, like a tel number or a SIP address. Some countries keep this list private, so it may not be in the public phone book.

sections.title: The Two Registrations
sections.content:
Two registrations are made. Both use the Enumservice name and type "pstn" and the intended usage COMMON.

  • Subtype tel, URI scheme tel:. The URIs may contain number portability data as specified in RFC 4694.
  • Subtype sip, URI scheme sip:.

Both indicate that the remote resource can be reached through the URI scheme to start a telecommunication session with the PSTN, which may include two-way voice or other communications. Both note that a Number Portability Dip Indicator (npdi) should be used in practice. IANA registers the type and both subtypes in the Enumservice registry from RFC 3761.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two versions of the label. One hands out a plain phone number, the other hands out an internet-call address. Both lead to the regular phone network.

sections.title: Example NAPTR Records
sections.content:
All examples use the origin 3.2.1.0.5.5.5.5.1.2.1.e164.arpa., with order 10 and preference 100 and the flag u.

  • Ported number, tel: E2U+pstn:tel returns tel:+1-215-555-0123;npdi;rn=+1-215-555-0199. The rn is the Routing Number. The npdi is included to prevent later lookups in legacy-style PSTN databases.
  • Ported number, sip: E2U+pstn:sip returns a SIP URI with the same npdi and rn at gw.example.com;user=phone. The conversion from tel to SIP URI follows RFC 3261 Section 19.1.6 and RFC 4694 Section 6.
  • Non-ported numbers use the same shapes with only npdi and no rn.

A fifth example uses the regular expression !(^.*)$!tel:\1;npdi!, where \1 is replaced by the number with its leading "+", here +1-215-555-0123. This shortens the record.
sections.plainLanguage: For a moved number the answer holds the phone number plus a note saying where it really is. For a number that did not move there is just the number and a note saying no need to check again.

sections.title: Implementation Recommendations
sections.content:
A query will likely return both E2U+sip and E2U+pstn records: one gives an address on an IP network (on-net) and the other an address on the PSTN (off-net). As with any ENUM query on e164.arpa, the application using the resolver decides which records to use. Implementers should build logic to choose by business, network or other rules, for example preferring the on-net record.

The RFC says tel URIs may be easier and more efficient than SIP URIs and may give somewhat smaller NAPTR records, which matters when hundreds of millions of records could go into the DNS. Regular expressions can shrink records further. The regular expression in the fifth example saves 11 bytes per record.
sections.plainLanguage: You may get two answers: an internet address and a phone-network address. Your software picks the better one using its own rules. Short answers help when there are millions of them.

sections.title: Call Processing Walkthroughs
sections.content:
Two walkthroughs show a calling application using the Enumservice. In the first, the dialed number is not available on-net. The user dials +1-215-555-0123, the application forms the name 3.2.1.0.5.5.5.5.1.2.1.e164.arpa, DNS returns an E2U+pstn:tel record with tel:+1-215-555-0123;npdi, and the application picks the nearest media gateway and routes the call.

In the second, the number is available both on-net and on the PSTN. DNS returns both an E2U+pstn and an E2U+sip record. The application tries the on-net SIP record first, setting up a SIP call to gw.example.com. If the IP route fails, it may use the pstn record as a fallback route to a media gateway connected to the PSTN.
sections.plainLanguage: You dial a number and the phone system looks it up. If there is an internet route it uses that first. If that fails it falls back to the regular phone network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If implementers use e164.arpa or another public domain for PSTN Enumservice data, anyone can see it anonymously. That is not qualitatively different from a telephone directory, but it makes access easier and leaves no trace of who accessed it. Third parties could harvest numbers to build lists for unsolicited telemarketing calls. Many countries have do-not-call registries or other legal mechanisms for such abuse.

Carriers and providers may choose not to publish in the public tree. They may use an internal ENUM routing database that only trusted elements such as softswitches and SIP proxy servers can query, or a carrier-only branch of E164.ARPA, should one be created. A phone number may reveal less identity than a sip or email address, but it is still public, so unwanted communication remains a risk.

Threats from ENUM's dependence on DNS, and the use of DNSSEC, are analyzed in RFC 3761. Threats to DNS itself are covered in RFC 3833.
sections.plainLanguage: If the list is public, people with bad intentions can copy numbers and make junk calls. Companies can keep their list private so only their own equipment can read it.
